query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Transforming the AM Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA to an ultrafine‐grained microstructure will promote formation of a dense duplex oxide scale (a protective Cr2O3 top layer with an adherent inner Al2O3 layer) that limits cation diffusion during high-temperature exposure. Without this microstructural modification, the alloy is prone to developing porous, non-uniform oxide layers (including deleterious spinel phases) that can spall and lead to catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built AM HEA with relatively coarse grains, which tend to form thicker, porous, nonprotective oxide layers with significant spinel content.
generation.intervention: Process the alloy to achieve an ultrafine-grained microstructure (via high strain-rate processing or laser cladding induced nanocrystallization) to increase grain boundary density.
generation.conditions: Exposures at elevated temperatures (e.g., 850 °C to 1050 °C) in oxidizing (e.g., air or O2-enriched) and reducing gas environments where cation diffusion and oxide scale integrity are critical.
generation.structural_mediator: The ultrafine-grained microstructure, providing abundant grain boundaries that serve as rapid diffusion paths for key alloying elements (notably Cr and Al) to form a continuous, duplex oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced grain boundary diffusion in the ultrafine-grained state promotes a rapid and uniform formation of a thin, compact Cr2O3 layer on the surface that acts as a barrier to outward cation transport, followed by the formation of an inner, adherent Al2O3 layer via inward oxygen diffusion. This complete, protective duplex structure reduces further oxidation and delays catastrophic spallation failure. In contrast, the coarse-grained state favors uneven oxidation kinetics leading to thicker, porous, and brittle spinel layers that undermine scale adhesion.
generation.predicted_outcome: The ultrafine-grained material will exhibit a significantly thinner, more uniform, and adherent duplex oxide scale with reduced presence of secondary spinel phases. This should translate into slower overall oxidation kinetics and delayed or reduced onset of catastrophic failure compared to the as-built coarse-grained baseline.
generation.baseline: The as-built coarse-grained AM HEA that typically forms a thick, porous, and multilayered oxide scale with brittle spinel regions, promoting localized oxidation, crack formation, and eventual catastrophic spallation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under high-temperature oxidation/reduction exposures between approximately 850 °C and 1050 °C, where cation diffusion through the oxide scale controls degradation, but may not apply at lower temperatures or under conditions where phase transformations dominate.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative differences in oxide scale thickness and the rate of failure (spallation or catastrophic cracking) between ultrafine-grained and coarse-grained states remain to be determined. The influence of simultaneous reducing gas exposure on the duplex scale integrity also requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the AM Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA: one in the as-built (coarse-grained) state and one processed to achieve an ultrafine-grained microstructure. Expose both sets to controlled high-temperature oxidation/reduction environments (850–1050 °C) for similar durations. Use techniques such as cross-sectional SEM/EDS and XRD to characterize the oxide scale composition, thickness, uniformity, and adhesion, and perform mechanical testing to monitor onset of catastrophic failure.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and layer uniformity (via SEM cross-sectional imaging)
Phase identification of oxide layers (via XRD)
Elemental mapping (via EDS) to confirm the presence of duplex Cr2O3 and Al2O3 layers versus spinel phases
Mechanical adhesion/cracking analysis to evaluate catastrophic failure onset
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultrafine-grained samples do not form a thinner, more continuous duplex oxide scale (with evident Cr2O3/Al2O3 layering) and do not show an improvement in resistance to catastrophic failure compared to as-built samples, then the hypothesis that ultrafine-grained microstructure governs protective scale formation and slows degradation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 2 shows the cross-sectional microstructure of the oxide scale formed on the Innovation Alloy, together with the high-magnification interfacial details. To clarify the effects of alloying and laser-cladding-induced nanocrystallization on oxide-scale evolution, the cross-sectional morphologies of the three alloys after oxidation at 900 °C for 120 h were compared. As shown in Figure 2a, the Base Alloy develops a thick, porous, and multilayered oxide scale with a total thickness of approximately 15.2 μm (marked by arrows), indicating rapid oxidation and limited protective capability. In contrast, the Synergy Alloy forms a much thinner and more continuous scale (approximately 1.8 μm, Figure 2b), demonstrating the beneficial role of Cr, Co, and Mn in improving scale compactness. The most compact and thinnest oxide structure is observed for the Innovation Alloy (Figure 2c), which exhibits a dense and adherent scale with a thickness of only 450 nm. This optimized architecture, featuring a distinct MnCr2O4/ Al2O3 duplex layer, effectively inhibits further oxygen ingress and metal-cation outward diffusion, thereby accounting for the markedly improved oxidation resistance of the design

cited_evidence.text: Figures 8–10 show the cross section BSE images of the oxidized samples along with their EDS elemental mapping. The elemental distribution indicates the formation of the mixed oxides in the as-cast sample oxidized at elevated temperatures, 850, 950, and 1050 °C, due to the slow diffusion of elements through GBs owing to the low number of GBs. Ultrafine grain size promotes the diffusion phenomenon owing to the higher number of GBs, which offer adequate diffusion paths for the mobility of ionic species. As-cast sample oxidized at 850 °C exhibits an oxide layer comprising Cr-, Fe-, and Co-rich oxides with a minor amount of Al2O3. However, the oxide layer formed on the surface of ultrafine-grained samples oxidized at 850 °C consists of a thin Cr2O3 layer followed by aluminum-rich inner oxides. The formation of chromia on the alloy’s surface is due to the outward diffusion of Cr ions through GBs, while alumina grows at the bottom-most oxide owing to the inward diffusion of O ions. The surface of as-cast samples oxidized at 950–1050 °C consists of an alumina layer at the bottom with appropriate fractions of Cr-, Fe-, and Co-rich oxides on the upper part of the scale. reading.lever: Process the AM alloy to an ultrafine-grained state that promotes a dense, duplex (Cr2O3/Al2O3) oxide scale limiting cation diffusion at high temperatures.
reading.why: Ultrafine-grained architecture has been shown in similar HEA systems to enhance protective scale formation and adhesion, directly countering degradation and catastrophic failure.
